notes.short: Wrong gain, righteousness; then righteous, wicked
notes.about: The two sayings cross: wrong gain, then righteousness; then the righteous, then the wicked. Read together, the second can give the reason for the first: the LORD keeps the righteous from hunger, and He turns away what the wicked crave.

lines.words: Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing,
but righteousness brings deliverance from death.
The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry,
but He denies the craving of the wicked.

original.note: In Hebrew the ill-gotten treasures are treasures of wickedness (resha); the last line speaks of the wicked (resha'im).

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the members of verse 3 stand in chiastic relation to those of verse 2. Henry pairs them the same way and takes the second verse as the reason for the first: treasures of wickedness profit nothing because God casts away the substance of the wicked, and righteousness delivers from death because the LORD will not let the righteous famish.

cites.quote: Another proverb, the members of which stand in chiastic relation to those of the preceding
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: These two verses speak to the same purport, and the latter may be the reason of the former. … the reason is because God casts away the substance of the wicked … For the Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish … and so their righteousness delivers from death
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The righteous kept from hunger, the wicked refused
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. The LORD keeps the righteous from going hungry, but He refuses the wicked what they crave.

lines.words: The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry,
but He denies the craving of the wicked.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line speaks of the appetite (nefesh) of the righteous, and the second answers with the craving (havvah) of the wicked.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) takes the craving of the wicked as the parallel of the appetite of the righteous: God satisfies the one and pushes the other back. Clarke: the righteous have God for their feeder, while on the contrary the wicked lose what they misuse.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the last line: one reads it of the wicked losing the goods they misuse, the other of their craving refused, as the BSB has it.

cites.quote: The parallel הוּה … means the desire … God gives satisfaction to the soul of the righteous, viz., in granting blessings. The desire of the wicked He does not suffer to be accomplished
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The righteous have God for their feeder; and because of his infinite bounty, they can never famish for want of the bread of life. On the contrary, the wicked are often, in the course of his providence, deprived of the property of which they make a bad use.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The fool's delight and the wise man's, set opposite
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: the fool against the man of understanding, shameful conduct against wisdom. Many read the first line's delight as carried into the second, so that wisdom is the wise man's pleasure as wrongdoing is the fool's.

lines.words: The fool delights in shameful conduct,
but a man of understanding has wisdom.

original.note: In Hebrew the order turns round in the second line: fool, then wickedness; wisdom, then man of understanding.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says sinful conduct is sport to the fool and wisdom to the man of understanding, and that the two sides of the contrast are set crosswise within the verse. So Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), J. W. Nutt (Ellicott) and E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes): sin or mischief is the fool's pleasure, wisdom the wise man's.

cites.quote: Sinful conduct appears to the fool, who places himself above the solemnity of the moral law, as sport; and wisdom, on the contrary, (appears as sport) to a man of understanding. ... The subjects of the antithesis chiastically combine within the verse
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Sin is the pleasure of the wicked; wisdom that of the good.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Rather, But wisdom ( is sport ) to a man of understanding, i.e., one rejoices in mischief, the other ... in wise thoughts and deeds.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: As the fool finds his sport in doing mischief, so the man of understanding finds in wisdom his truest refreshment and delight.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Oppress the poor, taunt God; help them, honor Him
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. To oppress the poor is to taunt the God who made them; to be kind to the needy is to honor Him. How a man treats the poor is how he treats their Maker.

lines.words: Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker,
but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him.

notes.evidence: Henry: God reckons Himself affronted by the wrongs done to the poor, and honored by the kindnesses done to them, which He takes as done to Himself; so those who truly honor God show it by compassion to the poor.
notes.limit: The last line can also be read the other way round: whoever honors God shows it by kindness to the needy. Either way it answers the first line with its opposite.

cites.quote: He reckons himself affronted in the injuries that are done them. … He reckons himself honoured in the kindnesses that are done them; he takes them as done to himself … Those therefore that have any true honour for God will show it by compassion to the poor
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: A good name, then favor: both worth more than wealth
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. A good name is answered by favor, more desirable by better, and great riches by silver and gold: a good name and the love of others are worth more than wealth.

lines.words: A good name is more desirable than great riches;
favor is better than silver and gold.

original.note: In Hebrew the verse opens with the word for chosen and closes with the word for good, so the two verdicts frame it; the first line says only name, meaning a good name.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls favor the parallel of name, and the verse's first word, chosen, and its last, good, the parallel predicates, set crosswise in the Hebrew. He takes favor as being beloved, and name by itself as a good name.

cites.quote: The proverb is constructed chiastically; the commencing word נבחר (cf. Pro 21:3), and the concluding word טוב, are the parallel predicates … The parallel חן signifies grace and favour (being beloved)
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Whip and bridle for beasts, the rod for fools
notes.about: The two lines are built alike: a tool, then the one it is for. The first names two beasts that need correcting and holding in. The second sets fools beside them, so the rod fits a fool as the whip and bridle fit the horse and the donkey.

lines.words: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey,
and a rod for the backs of fools!

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): as whip and bridle are useful and needed, so is a rod. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): the rod is as much needed by fools as whips and bridles by beasts. Clarke: correction suits a fool as a whip a horse, or a bridle an ass. Henry: as an unbroken horse needs a whip and an ass a bridle, so a man who will not be guided must be corrected and held back.

cites.quote: As whip and bridle are both serviceable and necessary, so also serviceable and necessary is a rod
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The rod is as much needed by fools and as well suited to them, as whips and bridles are for beasts.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Correction is as suitable to a fool, as a whip is for a horse, or a bridle for an ass.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Wicked men are compared to the horse and the ass, so brutish are they, so unreasonable, so unruly … A horse unbroken needs a whip for correction, and an ass a bridle for direction and to check him when he would turn out of the way; so a vicious man, who will not be under the guidance and restraint of religion and reason, ought to be whipped and bridled
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Six things the LORD hates, then seven
notes.about: The verse speaks of six things the LORD hates, then raises the count to seven, and the next three verses list all seven. Many read the last, “one who stirs up discord among brothers,” as the one most stressed, worse than the rest.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: six things that the LORD hates, seven
figure.means: a list of what the LORD hates, rising to a seventh, the worst of all

notes.evidence: Henry finds the seventh especially meant, since the count is six, yea, seven. J. W. Nutt (Ellicott) says God hates six things and the seventh worse than all, a numerical proverb raising the first number by one; E. H. Plumptre (Barnes' Notes) sees the Hebrew form of climax. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a numerical proverb, the seventh the height of what God hates.
notes.limit: The seventh is read as the worst, not as the only one the LORD hates: the count here is exact, and all seven are detestable to Him.

cites.quote: the last of them (which, being the seventh, seems especially to be intended, because he says they are six, yea, seven) is part of his character, that he sows discord
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He hates six things, but the seventh worse than all. This numerical form of proverb ... in all these instances the number first named is increased afterwards by one.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: With the recognized Hebrew form of climax ... the teacher here enumerates six qualities as detestable, and the seventh as worse than all (seven represents completeness), but all the seven in this instance belong to one man
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The thought that no vice is a greater abomination to God than the (in fact satanical) striving to set men at variance who love one another, clothes itself in the form of the numerical proverb ... the seven are to be numbered separately, and the seventh is the non plus ultra of all that is hated by God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Three things, then four: the list builds to the last
notes.about: Agur names three things too wonderful for him, then raises the count to four. The four ways follow in the next verse, and the saying turns on the last of them, “the way of a man with a maiden”; the first three serve to set it off.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: three things too wonderful for me, four
figure.means: the count climbs from three to four, and the weight falls on the fourth thing named

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the saying another numerical proverb and says its turning point lies in the fourth thing: the other three lead to it and serve only as a foil to it. Matthew Henry says the first three are things of nature, given only as comparisons to shed light on the last.
notes.limit: The note claims only how the count builds. What the fourth way means, and what the four ways share, is read in more than one way.

cites.quote: The following proverb, again a numerical proverb, begins with the eagle, mentioned in the last line of the foregoing ... The turning-point lies in the fourth; to that point the other three expressions gravitate, which have not an object in themselves, but are only as folie to the fourth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: An account of four things that are unsearchable, too wonderful to be fully known. And here, 1. The first three are natural things, and are only designed as comparisons for the illustration of the last.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Honor the LORD with wealth, with firstfruits
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: honor the LORD with your wealth, and with the firstfruits of all your harvest.

lines.words: Honor the LORD with your wealth
and with the firstfruits of all your harvest;

pairs: the firstfruits of all your harvest
notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his examples of synonymous parallel lines, and says such lines are made of synonymous terms.

cites.quote: Honour Jehovah with thy riches; And with the first fruits of all thine increase. Prov. iii. 9. ... In the foregoing examples may be observed the different degrees of Synonymous Parallelism. The Parallel Lines sometimes consist of three or more Synonymous terms; sometimes of two
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

notes.short: Six things, seven, and then the list
notes.about: A number is given, then a greater one, and then the list follows line by line in the same build: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a scheming heart, feet quick to evil, a false witness, and one who stirs up discord.

lines.words: There are six things that the LORD hates,
seven that are detestable to Him:
haughty eyes,
a lying tongue,
hands that shed innocent blood,
a heart that devises wicked schemes,
feet that run swiftly to evil,
a false witness who gives false testimony,
and one who stirs up discord among brothers.

notes.evidence: Lowth says that where a set number is given twice over for an open one, the list of particulars that follows naturally makes the lines parallel, of the synthetic kind and no other; he gives these verses as an example of it.

cites.quote: Of the same sort of Parallelism are those passages, frequent in the Poetic Books, where a Definite number is twice put for an Indefinite; this being followed by an enumeration of particulars naturally throws the sentences into a Parallelism, which cannot be of any other than the Synthetic kind. ... Prov. vi. 16-19.
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

notes.short: A wise son, a foolish son: joy and grief
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: wise and foolish, joy and grief, father and mother. Each line names one parent, but the joy and the grief can be read as belonging to both.

lines.words: A wise son brings joy to his father,
but a foolish son grief to his mother.

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives the verse under his heading Antithetic, or Opposite: lines whose words are contrasted, opposed in sense. Lowth says every word has its opposite, father and mother included. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sets this antithetic proverb beside similar ones whose lines say the same thing, and says its two lines supply each other.
notes.limit: Pairing father with mother does not mean that only one parent rejoices and only the other grieves.

cites.quote: This is when the words are contrasted in the two or more lines, being opposed in sense the one to the other. Pro 10:1 . - “A wise son maketh a glad father ; But a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother ”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Where every word hath its opposite: for the terms father and mother are, as the Logicians say, relatively opposite.
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

cites.quote: Similar proverbs are found further on, but consisting of synonymous parallel members ... the division lies nearer in the synonymous distichs, and is there less liable to be misunderstood than in the antithetic. ... The idea of the parents is in this way only separated, and the two members stand in suppletive interchangeable relationship.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A blessed memory, a name that rots
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. Memory and name mean the same, but the righteous and the wicked, blessing and rot, are set against each other: one is remembered with thanks, the other's name decays.

lines.words: The memory of the righteous is a blessing,
but the name of the wicked will rot.

notes.evidence: Lowth says the verse has only two opposed terms, for memory and name are synonymous. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the remembrance of the righteous endures, while the name of the godless, on the contrary, becomes corrupt.

cites.quote: Here there are only two Antithetic terms: for memory and name are Synonymous.
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

cites.quote: The remembrance of the righteous endures after his death, for he is thought of with thankfulness ... because his works, rich in blessing, continue; the name of the godless, on the contrary, far from continuing fresh and green ... after his departure, becomes corrupt
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Gives and gains, withholds and grows poor
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: one gives freely, another withholds. Each line also sets its own two parts against each other, giving yet gaining more, and holding back only to become poor.

lines.words: One gives freely, yet gains even more;
another withholds what is right, only to become poor.

notes.evidence: Lowth calls this proverb a kind of double antithesis: one between the two lines, and a lesser one between the two parts of each line.

cites.quote: Here there is a kind of double Antithesis; one between the two lines themselves; and likewise a subordinate opposition between the two parts of each.
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

notes.short: One pretends to be rich, another to be poor
notes.about: The second half answers the first with its opposite: one pretends to be rich but has nothing; another pretends to be poor yet has great wealth.

lines.words: One pretends to be rich, but has nothing;
another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his first examples of antithetic lines. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): men act hypocritically in opposite ways.

cites.quote: The Antithetic parallelism is the next that I shall specify, when a thing is illustrated by its contrary being opposed to it. ... of which the following are examples ... There is who maketh himself rich, and wanteth all things; Who maketh himself poor, yet hath much wealth.
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

cites.quote: In opposite ways men act hypocritically for gain of honor or wealth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The lot is cast, but the LORD decides
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite, though no single word stands against another. The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD: what looks like chance is the LORD’s doing.

lines.words: The lot is cast into the lap,
but its every decision is from the LORD.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this proverb as one where the sense is opposed without any opposed terms: the event seems to be chance, but is really the direction of Providence.

cites.quote: In the following there is much the same opposition of sentiment, without any contraposition of terms at all: ... The lot is cast into the lap; But the whole determination of it is from Jehovah. ... That is, the event seems to be the work of Chance; but is really the direction of Providence.
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

notes.short: The son's heart and lips around the father's joy
notes.about: The first line speaks of the son's wise heart and the last of his lips speaking what is right. The two lines between tell of the father's joy: his own heart and his inmost being rejoice.

lines.words: My son, if your heart is wise,
my own heart will indeed rejoice.
My inmost being will rejoice
when your lips speak what is right.

notes.evidence: Jebb gives these verses as an example of what he calls the introverted parallelism: stanzas in which, he says, the first and last lines are parallel, and so are the second and the next to last.

cites.quote: whatever be the number of lines, the first line shall be parallel with the last; the second with the penultimate; and so throughout, in an order that looks inward ... This may be called the introverted parallelism: My son, if thine heart be wise; My heart also shall rejoice; Yea, my reins shall rejoice; When thy lips speak right things. Prov. xxiii. 15, 16.
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb

notes.short: A friend's wounds, an enemy's kisses
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: the wounds of a friend against the kisses of an enemy, faithful against deceitful.

lines.words: The wounds of a friend are faithful,
but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his examples of antithetic parallelism, where a thing is illustrated by its contrary. Bullinger gives it under his heading Antithetic, or Opposite, where lines are opposed in sense. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sets the faithful strokes of one who loves us against the kisses of an enemy.

cites.quote: The Antithetic parallelism is the next that I shall specify, when a thing is illustrated by its contrary being opposed to it. This is not confined to any particular form: for sentiments are opposed to sentiments, words to words, singulars to singulars, plurals to plurals, &c. of which the following are examples: The blows of a friend are faithful; But the kisses of an enemy are treacherous.
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

cites.quote: This is when the words are contrasted in the two or more lines, being opposed in sense the one to the other. ... Faithful are the wounds of a friend, But deceitful are the kisses of an enemy
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This, then, is the contrast, that the strokes inflicted by one who truly loves us, although they tear into our flesh ... yet are faithful ... on the contrary, the enemy covers over with kisses him to whom he wishes all evil.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Full, honey is loathed; hungry, bitter is sweet
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite: the soul that is full and the hungry soul, honey that is loathed and any bitter thing that is sweet.

lines.words: The soul that is full loathes honey,
but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his first examples of antithetic lines, where a thing is set off by its contrary.

cites.quote: The Antithetic parallelism is the next that I shall specify, when a thing is illustrated by its contrary being opposed to it. ... of which the following are examples: ... The cloyed will trample upon an honey-comb; But to the hungry every bitter thing is sweet
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

notes.short: A rich man wise in his own eyes, a poor man who sees
notes.about: The two halves set a rich man who is wise in his own eyes against a poor man with discernment, who sees through him.

lines.words: A rich man is wise in his own eyes,
but a poor man with discernment sees through him.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his first examples of antithetic lines, where a thing is set off by its contrary.

cites.quote: The Antithetic parallelism is the next that I shall specify, when a thing is illustrated by its contrary being opposed to it. ... of which the following are examples: ... The rich man is wise in his own eyes, But the poor man that hath discernment to trace him out will despise him.
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

notes.short: The ruler’s favor set against the LORD
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. The two lines turn chiefly on the ruler and the LORD, and the whole saying sets seeking a ruler’s favor against the LORD, from whom justice comes.

lines.words: Many seek the ruler’s favor,
but a man receives justice from the LORD.

notes.evidence: Lowth says the opposition in this proverb lies chiefly between the ruler and the LORD, and also in the sense of the whole.

cites.quote: Where the opposition is chiefly between the single terms the Prince, and Jehovah: but there is an opposition likewise in the general sentiment
cites.read: the 1795 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/isaiahnewtransla01lowt

notes.short: The noble wife's praise, set out letter by letter
notes.about: In Hebrew the 22 verses of this poem on the noble wife, verses 10 to 31, begin with the letters of the alphabet in order, from the first letter to the last. The pattern may have been meant to help readers learn the poem by heart.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.means: In Hebrew this opens a poem whose 22 verses begin with the letters of the alphabet in order, ending with the last letter in verse 31.

original.note: In Hebrew verse 10 opens with eshet, “wife”, whose first letter, aleph, is the first of the alphabet.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 10 to 31 under Acrostichion as a perfect alphabetical acrostic. Clarke: each verse begins with the next Hebrew letter, aleph in verse 10 to tau in verse 31. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) and Henry: the verses begin with the letters in order. Poole says the order calls for careful remembrance; Nutt (Ellicott), that it may have made the poem easier to learn by heart.

cites.quote: is a perfect alphabetical Acrostic, marking and calling our attention to this song in praise of a virtuous woman.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This and the following verses are acrostic, each beginning with a consecutive letter of the Hebrew alphabet: Pro 31:10, א aleph; Pro 31:11, ב beth; Pro 31:12, ג gimel; and so on to the end of the chapter, the last verse of which has the letter ת tau.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In Hebrew the verses begin with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This description of the virtuous woman is designed to show what wives the women should make and what wives the men should choose; it consists of twenty-two verses, each beginning with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet in order, as some of the Psalms
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This is written in the form of an acrostic, the twenty-two verses composing it each commencing with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This may have been done, as in the case of several of the psalms, which are of a didactic character (e.g., 25, 34, 37, 119), to render it more easy for committal to memory.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: And here he lays down several characters or qualifications of an excellent wife, which are here delivered in alphabetical order, each verse beginning with a several and the succeeding letter of the Hebrew alphabet; which method is used in some, and but in a few places of Scripture, to oblige us to the more diligent consideration and careful remembrance of them
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/proverbs/31.htm
